clue.text: Relaxed and thinking of England?

definitions.meaning: easy-going and unflustered, not bothered by much
from the old joke advice to 'lie back and think of England', so someone thinking of England is lying back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie back and think of England' is a jocular British phrase for enduring something passively; the question mark flags the playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy-going people are casually described with this compound adjective, literally meaning reclined.

clue.text: Propriety of member having sex being nameless

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

indicators.note: without a name means the abbreviation N, for name, is dropped

parts.note: intimacy is a polite word for sex

explanation.surface: Questioning the decency of a member of parliament who has an affair anonymously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nameless' drops N, the abbreviation for name, from INTIMACY; 'having' and 'being' are links. The surface's member of parliament is really a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawfulness or rightful standing, the quality of being proper and allowed, is a close synonym for propriety.

clue.text: I abandon immediate problem in part payment

parts.note: inst. is short for instant, which means immediate (in old business letters, 'the 10th inst.')

indicators.note: the letter I is left behind, dropped from the word for an illness

parts.note: an ailment is a health problem

explanation.surface: Someone gives up an urgent difficulty by paying in stages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandon' drops the I from AILMENT, leaving ALMENT; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: One of a series of payments spread over time is a portion of the total paid.

clue.text: See 26
Bill or Nick?

parts.note: what looks like two men's names are British slang for the police: the Old Bill, and the nick, a police station

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Old Bill' is British slang for the police, and 'the nick' is slang for a police station.
explanation.definitionFit: A police force is a body of officers, and both slang terms refer to the police.

clue.text: Case for stations?

definitions.meaning: a law case is a legal ... brought against someone
the word that goes before 'stations' in the naval call to battle positions

explanation.walkthrough: 'Action stations!' is the order sending a ship's crew to their battle posts; the question mark warns that the second definition fills a phrase rather than defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawsuit is known formally as a legal proceeding of this name, and the word also completes the battle-readiness call.

clue.text: Send parcel to a needlewoman

indicators.note: to send letters means to dispatch them in a new order, rearranging them

explanation.surface: Instructions to post a package to a seamstress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send' rearranges PARCEL TO A. The definition plays on Cleopatra's Needle, the Egyptian obelisk on London's Victoria Embankment.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian queen has a London obelisk named after her, the Needle, so she is jokingly a woman with a needle.

clue.text: Leisure for love found by Puck

definitions.meaning: follows the word 'love-in-' to name the flower Puck fetches

explanation.walkthrough: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, Puck is sent for the flower love-in-idleness, whose juice makes people fall in love.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing nothing, being at rest, is a state of leisure, and the word also ends the flower's name.

clue.text: See 7
Spirit like this is found in Ealing production

indicators.note: says the short phrase meaning 'like this' is placed within the rearranged studio name
a production of Ealing reworks the letters of that word into a new order

parts.note: so means in this way, like this

explanation.surface: A tipple of the sort shown on screen turns up in a film made by Ealing Studios.
explanation.walkthrough: 'production' rearranges EALING into GALINE, and 'found in' puts SO into it; 'is' is a link. Ealing is the west London film studio famous for comedies, and spirit here is American motor fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor spirit is the British name for fuel that Americans call by this word, so it is a spirit in that sense.

clue.text: Dislike Greece?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and, by extension, the underworld itself, the infernal regions
as means like, in the manner of

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they dislike Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dislike' must be split into 'Dis' and 'like'; the single word hides both pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The country's own name in Greek, used in English poetically and on its stamps.

clue.text: Medical centre on right lines having operating theatre outside

indicators.note: the rearranged theatre goes round the abbreviation and the lines
operating on the letters of theatre works them into a new order

parts.note: leys are ley lines, alignments said to link ancient sites

explanation.surface: A clinic on the right lines has its operating theatre around the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operating' rearranges THEATRE into HATREET, and 'outside' puts it round the other pieces; 'on' and 'having' are links. Harley Street in London is famous for private doctors; ley lines are supposed ancient alignments.
explanation.definitionFit: This London street is famous for private medical practices, so it is the centre of British medicine.

clue.text: Temporary accommodation for cast in trouble with walkabout

indicators.note: the long walk takes the rearranged letters into its middle, holding them with it

parts.note: a tramp is a long walk, a hike on foot

indicators.note: cast in trouble means those letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A theatre company in difficulties is put up in makeshift lodgings while on tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges CAST IN into ANSITC, and 'with' has the walk hold it. The theatrical cast is a red herring: no actors are involved.
explanation.definitionFit: A camp holding refugees or soldiers on the move houses them only for a while, so it is temporary accommodation.

clue.text: Unnatural liar, if I act differently

indicators.note: the letters, acted out another way, are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A liar admits that acting another way would be fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made by people rather than occurring naturally is man-made, the opposite of natural.

clue.text: Inflates good result that may open disastrously

indicators.note: the fodder's result is the letters worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: the printed words carry an extra IN at the start of 'Inflates'; the setter's intended fodder is the remaining FLATES plus GOOD

explanation.surface: Someone pumps up a good outcome that could burst open with terrible effect.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram needs FLATES GOOD; the printed 'Inflates' carries an extra IN, which the setter seems to have meant as part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluice gates holding back water cause a disaster when opened, hence the image of letting loose a flood.

clue.text: Copy number from La Bohème?

parts.note: Mimì is the heroine of Puccini's opera La Bohème
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone wants a copy of a song from Puccini's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' looks like a song from the opera, but it is just the numeral C; the opera supplies its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate someone is to copy their voice or manner, and that is the verb here.

clue.text: Acrobatic movement by business group with man in it

indicators.note: the abbreviation and the man go inside the business group, 'it' referring to that group

parts.note: a cartel is an association of businesses that fixes prices
he is a male person

explanation.surface: A gymnastic move performed by a trade association with a man in its midst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in it' places the pieces inside the business group, 'it' pointing back to that group; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideways handspring with arms and legs extended like spokes is a gymnastic turn.

clue.text: 4 is around at time for two parties

indicators.note: the police nickname goes round the outside of the other pieces

parts.note: 4-down is the police force, nicknamed the Old Bill in British slang
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: The police are around at some point to deal with a two-sided arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Bill is British slang for the police, the answer to 4-down. 'is around' wraps that nickname round the other pieces; 'parties' suggests a celebration but means the sides to an agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: An agreement between two sides, such as a treaty between two countries, is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Little money for get-together done without devolution

parts.note: a cent is a coin of small value, a hundredth of a dollar or euro
a rally is a mass gathering or meeting

explanation.surface: A small sum is collected for a meeting held without handing powers to the regions.
explanation.definitionFit: Devolution passes power to regions, so government done without it is run from the middle.

clue.text: All ready for setter's take off, chum?

parts.note: the setter is I, and 'setter's' (setter is) turned into a question reads 'am I'
to go is to set off or leave

explanation.surface: Asking whether everything is ready for the crossword setter's departure, mate?
explanation.walkthrough: The answer read as a question, 'Am I go?', asks whether the setter is all ready to take off; 'All ready for' frames that question and the question mark marks it.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Spanish, the word is a friendly name for a friend or pal.

clue.text: Surveillance in place of press covering fury with model

indicators.note: the London district wraps round the anger and the car model

parts.note: Wapping in east London became home to Murdoch's newspaper presses in 1986, after a famous dispute
ire is anger, fury
the Model T was Henry Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: Snooping goes on in a newspaper district where the press hides anger behind a model.
explanation.walkthrough: Wapping is the east London district where The Times and The Sun moved their printing in 1986. 'covering' wraps it round the pieces; 'in' is a link, and 'press' is newspapers, not squeezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Listening in on telephone lines is a kind of covert watching or monitoring.

clue.text: Overture's key in concert

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: the musical key is placed inside the word for a concert

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at London's BBC Proms
E is one of the musical keys

explanation.surface: An overture written in a particular key for a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are London's summer season of promenade concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: An introduction or preface to a book or speech is a kind of overture.

clue.text: Pilgrimage held on first of June

parts.note: had means held, possessed

indicators.note: takes only the opening letter of the month's name

explanation.surface: A religious journey was held at the start of June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link; the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca is also spelt hajj.
explanation.definitionFit: The annual Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca has this spelling as one of its variants.

clue.text: What Capone did on his tax return, like?

parts.note: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster
Capone was finally jailed for tax evasion, so he told untruths on his returns

explanation.surface: A question about what the Chicago gangster got up to when filing his taxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What' is a link. Al Capone escaped conviction for his violent crimes but was jailed in 1931 for tax evasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are related or similar in kind are said to be akin, comparable, alike.

clue.text: Fellow into crime, one seeking pleasure

indicators.note: the university fellow is placed inside the word for a robbery

parts.note: a heist is a robbery, a crime
a don is a university fellow or tutor

explanation.surface: A man gets involved in a robbery because he wants a good time.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose life is devoted to enjoyment and indulgence is a pleasure-seeker of this kind.

clue.text: Dickensian beauties heard as accompaniment to Santa Claus

parts.note: Alfred Jingle is a con man in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers

indicators.note: said out loud, the word for pretty women sounds like ringing chimes

parts.note: belles are beautiful women

explanation.surface: Lovely women from a Dickens novel, overheard escorting Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Jingle is a rogue in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers; 'heard' makes BELLES sound as BELLS.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Christmas song, and the sleigh bells it describes, go along with Santa on his rounds.

clue.text: I must turn left at the Guardian's prompting

indicators.note: the letters of 'I must' turn around into a new order

parts.note: the newspaper speaks of itself as we, so what belongs to it is ours, giving us

explanation.surface: A Guardian editorial nudge: I really have to turn left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' rearranges I MUST into STIMU; 'at' is a link. The clue appeared in the Guardian, which calls itself 'us'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur or incentive that urges action is a prompting, a nudge to do something.
